**Detection must decide both what exists and where it is.** Two-stage detectors first propose regions and then classify/refine them. Single-stage detectors predict object classes and boxes more directly across image features. DETR-style models use learned object queries and set prediction, trained with a one-to-one matching objective. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12872)

**Why duplicate predictions arise.** Many nearby anchors or locations can predict the same object. Traditional pipelines often use NMS to keep a strong box and suppress redundant overlaps. That postprocessing has thresholds and can confuse nearby distinct objects.

**DETR changes the training assignment.** Match predicted objects to ground-truth objects using a bipartite cost based on classification and box quality. Hungarian matching chooses a one-to-one assignment. Matched predictions learn their targets; unmatched predictions learn the no-object outcome. This discourages producing many copies of the same object and enables the original end-to-end formulation without conventional NMS.

This does not mean every later model called DETR has identical architecture or no additional inference choices. Small-object performance, training convergence, resolution, query count, and feature design vary across variants.

Compare accuracy by object size, latency at the actual image resolution, memory, training cost, and crowded-scene behavior. “Single-stage” is not a guarantee of lower latency than every two-stage implementation, and a set-prediction objective is not proof of perfect duplicate elimination on every input.

**Technical details and references.**

Two-stage detectors first propose regions and then classify/refine them. Single-stage detectors predict classes and boxes densely in one pass; focal loss addresses the many easy background candidates. DETR uses a fixed set of learned object queries and matches predicted objects to ground truth during training. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12872) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.02002)

$$\hat\sigma=\arg\min_\sigma\sum_i\mathcal C(y_i,\hat y_{\sigma(i)}).$$

The matching cost combines class and box terms. Each target matches one prediction; unmatched predictions learn “no object,” discouraging duplicates without conventional NMS. This avoids hand-designed anchor assignment in original DETR, but does not imply every later transformer detector uses identical mechanisms. Compare small-object performance, convergence, latency, and recall; architecture family alone does not determine those outcomes.
